title: Homograph phishing defense
summary: Lookalike characters forge official domains to harvest signatures or seeds.

sections.heading: What it looks like
sections.body: Attackers swap visually similar characters into domains and pair them with ads or DMs. The UI can be pixel-perfect and even show fake balances.

sections.heading: How to spot it
sections.body: Type URLs or use bookmarks. Check certificate owners. Never click the top search ad for wallets/bridges. Hover links and inspect odd subdomains.

sections.heading: If you clicked
sections.body: Revoke approvals and move remaining funds. If you typed a seed, that wallet is burned—rescue to a brand-new seed only. Keep evidence for reports.

checklist: Cross-check on a second device for size
body: Lookalike characters forge official domains to harvest signatures or seeds.

title: Seed phrase complete guide
summary: Your seed is control of the assets. Anyone asking for it is hostile.

sections.heading: Backups
sections.body: Hand-write and re-check order; consider metal plates; split locations carefully. No photos, clouds, or chat apps.

sections.heading: Scams
sections.body: “Sync/verify/upgrade/unfreeze/airdrop” pages requesting 12/24 words. Fake Discord admins use the same script. Hardware “authenticity checkers” asking for seeds are fake.

sections.heading: Inheritance
sections.body: If nobody knows the plan, funds die with you. Use sealed instructions, lawyers, or multisig. On suspected leak, migrate immediately.

checklist: Tell the words to no one
Never enter them on a networked device
body: Your seed is control of the assets. Anyone asking for it is hostile.

title: Approve / allowance traps
summary: Approvals don’t move tokens immediately—they allow later drains, especially unlimited ones.

sections.heading: Mechanics
sections.body: ERC-20 transferFrom needs allowance. Infinite approvals are convenient; compromised spenders can empty you later. setApprovalForAll is the NFT equivalent.

sections.heading: Safe practice
sections.body: Exact allowances when possible; revoke routinely; test new protocols small. Watch airdrop sites that require Approve first.

sections.heading: Incident response
sections.body: Revoke and move funds. Prioritize spenders named in hack disclosures.

body: Approvals don’t move tokens immediately—they allow later drains, especially unlimited ones.

title: Fake wallet apps
summary: Clones appear in stores and sideload channels to steal seeds or remote-control devices.

sections.heading: Spotting fakes
sections.body: Match publisher names to official posts; beware brand-new apps ranking #1. Prefer links from the real site. Sideloaded APKs are riskier.

sections.heading: Hardening
sections.body: Keep OS updated; minimize plugins; consider a dedicated phone. Use hardware for size. Plan remote lock if the phone is lost.

sections.heading: After install
sections.body: If a seed was entered into a fake app, assume compromise and migrate on a clean device.

body: Clones appear in stores and sideload channels to steal seeds or remote-control devices.

title: Signature drainers & malicious permits
summary: No seed required—malicious structured signatures can authorize drains.

sections.heading: Tactics
sections.body: Fake mints/claims request setApprovalForAll, permits, or “logins.” Some payloads look blank. Bots sweep afterward.

sections.heading: Defense
sections.body: Clear-signing wallets, simulation, reject unknowns. Connect new sites with a burner first. Check domains.

sections.heading: Afterward
sections.body: Revoke, rescue funds, warn communities, check other chains for the same approvals.

checklist: Use a burner on new sites
body: No seed required—malicious structured signatures can authorize drains.

title: Fake support & social engineering
summary: After you post an error, impersonators DM “help” asking for remote access or seeds.

sections.heading: The playbook
sections.body: Cloned avatars, urgency, remote-control apps, or “safe contract” deposit instructions. Compromised friend accounts spread links too.

sections.heading: Rules
sections.body: Real teams rarely DM first for secrets. Use official tickets/public channels. Verify friends out-of-band.

sections.heading: Hygiene
sections.body: Never paste seeds in public channels—even “partially masked.”

body: After you post an error, impersonators DM “help” asking for remote access or seeds.

title: Bridge safety
summary: Bridges are top hack targets and phishing favorites. Faster is not safer by default.

sections.heading: Choosing
sections.body: Prefer canonical bridges from official docs. Vet fast bridges for audits and limits. Understand exit delays.

sections.heading: Operating
sections.body: Tiny end-to-end tests; verify destination token contracts; save hashes. Don’t treat in-flight exits as free margin.

sections.heading: Incidents
sections.body: On bridge hacks, follow official pause notices—not DM “migration scripts.”

body: Bridges are top hack targets and phishing favorites. Faster is not safer by default.

title: Device & browser hygiene
summary: Clipboard malware, fake extensions, and shared PCs are everyday theft paths.

sections.heading: Browser
sections.body: Dedicated crypto profile; minimal official extensions; bookmark sites. Use a clean machine for size.

sections.heading: System
sections.body: Patch OS; beware “airdrop tools”; avoid sketchy public chargers. Always re-check pasted addresses.

sections.heading: Layering
sections.body: Hot for daily, cold for savings, multisig for treasuries beats one super-wallet.

body: Clipboard malware, fake extensions, and shared PCs are everyday theft paths.
